extracted.intended_audience: high-school journalism students and student newspaper staff (editors, proofreaders, advertising managers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and editing a high-school newspaper: creating and enforcing a style sheet, page make-up and proofs, typographical/head rules, proofreading code, and planning advertising campaigns and copy. Covers editorial standards, production (galleys/dummy/page proofs), and ad strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and enforce a style sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: The high school paper must be consistent in punctuation, capitalization, spelling and general practices; a style book or style sheet should record the paper's chosen practices and all regular contributors must follow it rigidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style should grow from study of good journalistic usage and common student errors; the style sheet is not exhaustive and must evolve. The printer and staff must follow the adopted style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use full names on first reference; follow name-format rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Full names must be written the first time a person is mentioned; thereafter precede the last name by Mr. or Miss; if a boy student, repeat the last name only, never the first alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mr. John L. Foley and Dr. Frank M. Wheat, not Mr. Foley and Dr. Wheat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer active voice; avoid passive constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using the passive instead of the active voice in news writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'A cat stole across the street' rather than 'was seen walking across the street.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strong verbs; avoid unnecessary adjectives/adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using adjectives and adverbs when a live verb will do the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The horse dashed down the street,' not 'went swiftly down the street.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not put two items into one article
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid packing more than one distinct item or topic into a single article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep articles focused on a single news item or topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning leads with the time element
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not start a lead with a date or time element; prefer relative time references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'John Brown was elected president of the XYZ, December 21' rather than 'On December 21, John Brown was elected...' Use 'next Tuesday', 'yesterday' when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning leads with articles (the, an, a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not begin leads with 'the', 'an', or 'a'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads should open with stronger, more immediate elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never use first person as the reporter; avoid opinion in news
rubrics_metrics.description: Never use first person in a news article to mean the reporter; never comment or give an opinion in a news article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes words like 'our' used as reporter voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer relative time words; use dates sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Say 'next Tuesday', 'last Wednesday', 'tomorrow', 'yesterday' rather than the exact date whenever possible; use 'recently' sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides immediacy and reader context; reduces stale-looking copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use infinitive for expressing purpose (avoid 'in order to')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'in order that' or 'for the purpose of'; use the infinitive to denote purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'To determine fitness of candidates, the program committee will hold an examination' instead of 'For the purpose of determining...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Word usage: persons vs people and other choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specified preferred words (e.g., 'persons' not 'people').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The style sheet should list other recurring word preferences for consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization: conservative and rule-based
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize sparingly; do not capitalize titles after a name, departments, or subjects unless style warrants (e.g., 'United States' precedes department).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'John Smith has been elected captain of the freshman team' (not 'Captain of the Freshman Team'); 'Dr. Bice is head of the Latin department' (not 'Latin Department'); 'I study French, Latin, biology, and mathematics.' Capitalize names of clubs/societies but not the generic 'the club.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling: follow Webster; avoid simplified spellings
rubrics_metrics.description: No simplified spelling; when in doubt follow Webster's preferred spelling; no abbreviations in the body; never divide a monosyllable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special attention list: gray (not grey), practice (not practise), adviser, acknowledgment, judgment. Spell out streets and avenues in addresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerals: use figures for 100 and above
rubrics_metrics.description: Use figures for 100 and above in copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given for street ranges and numbering conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation: commas with appositives and other rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit comma between name and numerals (Mary Smith 727); use commas to set off nonrestrictive appositives but omit where restrictive; quotation marks must begin and end quoted material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In continuous quotations of 2+ paragraphs, open quotes at each paragraph start and end quotes only at the last paragraph; watch comma placement in appositives vs restrictive phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be terse; prefer appositives and past participles
rubrics_metrics.description: Write concisely; avoid unnecessary words. Use appositives and past participles rather than relative clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'John Brown, former Arista leader,' not 'John Brown, who was formerly an Arista leader.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Alumni and bylines formatting and other general rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Alumni news: write 'Bill Jones '24' with no comma between name and year; poems: appear over writer's name with class numerals; tabulate only long lists; never invert students' names in copy for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never write a student's name as 'Gray, John' in published copy (filing only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports style consistency and score/reporting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be consistent in sports formatting: yard-line and yard-pass notations, use '5 to 3' in body for scores (use '5—3' only in heads), follow New York Times for box-scores/line-ups; use smaller type for summaries/box-scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'on her 35-yard line; 20-yard forward pass; 50-yard breast stroke.' Use 6-point instead of 8-point for line-ups/box-scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head and subhead typographical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Head style and size are noted on the head schedule. Use drop-line (step) form for top heads unless directed otherwise; set subheads bold face center, upper and lower case, with no period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize first word in second line of box heads and italic heads; use single quotation marks in headlines where double quotes would be used in body; banks set pyramid style capitalization rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical style in body: no italic emphasis, limited bold
rubrics_metrics.description: No italicizing for emphasis; no bold face type in body except inserts; break full-column articles by at least two subheads; if a byline is used, set center body type; special despatches set center italics body type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No leading ever; brief news items or a single joke may fill a short column but prefer news items; no teasers or fillers on front page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banks and headline capitalization (pyramid style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set banks (short heads) in pyramid style upper and lower case: capitalize all words except a, an, and, as, but, if, or, the, and prepositions of four letters or less; write infinitives as 'to End, to Boom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No period after banks; use a dash instead of a semicolon in the bank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breakovers and jump-head formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use prescribed forms for continued/breakover lines: e.g., 'Continued on Page 3, Column 2' set bold face at bottom of the first break; 'Continued from Page 1, Column 5' for jump heads and check consistency between markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check (b) with (a) on dummy and page proof to avoid discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash usage rules for heads and articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a 3-em dash under all heads except editorial heads; 3-em dash centered below every single column bank; 3-em dash above and below 'Continued from Page...' lines; use a 5-em dash at the end of every article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow consistent dash sizing and placement to separate elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use single rules and horizontal rules for story separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a single rule for boxes and a single horizontal rule to cut off a story set in two or three columns from heads below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow typographical conventions to visually separate content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of page make-up: balance, cuts, and head arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange front pages using symmetrical balance or occult (irregular) balance as appropriate; avoid monotony from large top cuts by varying heads and arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises: clip NYT columns and arrange a front page to achieve symmetrical balance; if placing a three-column cut at top, vary heads below to avoid monotony; balance cuts as you see fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galley proofs: check completeness and correct errors with code
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofs are pulled, editor must check printed stories against 'Sent to Printer' list to ensure all copy is set; read proofs and mark corrections using the proofreader's code in the margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marks must be legible to the linotype operator; indicate corrections both at the line and in the margin; editor writes 'OK with corrections' and initials when read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making the dummy: materials and stepwise procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare dummy pages using ruled wrapping paper cut to page size, arrange proofs in numerical order, mark galleys with their number, strip margins, cut stories, pin top stories in place first, then paste story by story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pinning allows changes; don't clip all pieces at once to avoid loss; paste after confirming layout; follow planned column widths and depths exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dummy/compositor exactness: indicate all production details
rubrics_metrics.description: The dummy must go to the compositor exactly as expected: indicate date line, page numbers, breakovers, continued-on lines, heads, dashes, and any additions required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If lines are to be added, send typed copy labeled appropriately (e.g., 'add Arista'); do not expect compositor to solve layout problems without clear instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling columns too long or too short
rubrics_metrics.description: If a story is too long for a column, transpose or cut lines; if too short, add lines by rushing copy to the printer or use a filler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label added lines and ensure the dummy reflects exact appearance desired by the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page proofs: final check
rubrics_metrics.description: When page proofs arrive, check all heads and overall form; it's too late to correct line length errors at this stage; all corrections must be indicated in the margins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure breakovers, dates and page numbers match the dummy before approving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and use the proofreader's marks/code
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should learn the standard proofreader's code and use corresponding marginal marks for insert, take out, capitals, italics, spacing, transposition, movement, punctuation, and other corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a few common marks (punctuation, capitalization, insert/take out), then expand mastery; each correction must be marked both at the line and in the margin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice proofreading with galley proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice correcting galley proofs using a card to isolate lines; at first correct common errors only (punctuation, capitalization, missing words), expanding as skill grows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mark for each correction must appear in two places (line and margin), or operator will assume proof is OK.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof and revision workflow: return proofs with corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs showing errors must be returned to the linotype operator for correction; revised proofs should show no errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor's responsibility is to track sent-to-printer copy and ensure corrections are implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising: define goals for printed and oral ads
rubrics_metrics.description: A good printed advertisement should make its public see, read, believe, remember, and act; an oral advertisement should make the public hear, listen, believe, remember, and act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct ads with those five aims in mind; choose techniques appropriate to printed vs oral media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising: catch attention (Make Him See/Hear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Catch attention via novelty of headline, suggestion, startling slogan, picture, or spectacular devices (moving signs, sky writing, neon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines and visual devices should be novel and arresting to create initial contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising: hold attention (Make Him Read/Listen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold attention with sparkling concrete details that challenge need and imagination; appeal to interest, emotion, attitude, instinct, senses, reason, or special viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness and dramatic form help; human-interest writers excel at live advertising copy; avoid vague 'cotton wool statements.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising: inspire confidence (Make Him Believe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspire confidence by sincerity and demonstrated knowledge of the commodity; use testimonials and guarantees as devices to build trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the public feel the advertiser's efficiency and authority on the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising: be memorable (Make Him Remember)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a slogan or catch phrase linking the firm name with the commodity and reinforce it through repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Fairy Soap', 'All the news that's fit to print.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising: facilitate action (Make Him Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it easy for the customer to act by showing convenient purchase methods and aligning sales opportunities with customers' conditions (e.g., hours); consider easy payment plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of customers' lives (work hours, purchasing constraints) increases conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral advertising technique: make him hear and listen
rubrics_metrics.description: In oral ads, pique curiosity with novelty, use dramatic entrances or stage business, then hold attention with brief vivid details, pleasing voice, well-timed pauses, and personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For personal appeals, seize clues that reveal customer interest and adapt the pitch accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan advertising campaigns for the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan general campaigns at the start of term to sell subscriptions and specific pre-issue campaigns to sell single copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising for the paper must culminate in subscriptions sold and copies distributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Before campaign: know commodity, public, finances, and roster
rubrics_metrics.description: Before campaigning know what the paper publishes and its distinctive points, know the public (student body, faculty, alumni) including numbers, set the sum required to cover term costs, and prepare a roster with class numbers and names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed knowledge of commodity and audience enables targeted campaigns and budget planning.
